study.title: Mark 15 The condemnation, crucifixion and burial of Jesus
study.overview: Mark 15 presents the final stage of Jesus" passion: he is taken to Pilate, rejected by the crowd, mocked by the soldiers, crucified among criminals, abandoned on the cross, confessed by a centurion and finally buried by Joseph of Arimathea with the silent testimony of two women. The chapter highlights human injustice, the firmness of Jesus amid suffering, the fulfillment of the Scriptures and the irony of a King who reigns through the cross.

outline.title: Jesus before Pilate and the choice for Barrabas
outline.explanation: The Jewish leaders hand over Jesus to the Roman governor, who interrogates him about his royal identity. Though he recognizes the pressure and envy of the chief priests, Pilate goes to the multitude and releases Barabbas, delivering Jesus to be flogged and crucified.

outline.title: Scarnios, Cross Path and Crucifixion
outline.explanation: The soldiers treat Jesus as a false king, crowning him with thorns and humiliating him. He is taken to Golgotha, crucified between two evildoers, and the inscription on his accusation proclaims precisely the title that condemns him. On the cross, it continues to be mocked by all the groups present.

outline.title: Darkness, Jesus" cry and signs in death
outline.explanation: At noon, darkness covers the earth until the ninth hour. Jesus cries out to God and then dies crying out loud. The veil of the temple tears off, and the centurion recognizes that he was truly the Son of God. Some women watch from afar.

outline.title: Sepplication of Jesus and tomb witnesses
outline.explanation: On the day of preparation, Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council and hopeful of the Kingdom of God, asks Pilate for the body of Jesus. He burys him in a tomb of rock, and Mary Magdalene and Mary, the mother of Joseph, observe the place where Jesus was placed.

study.context: The text indicates that the Roman judgment begins very early at dawn and that Pilate remains in Jerusalem at the time of the Passover, as recorded by the notes. Also appears the practice of releasing a prisoner at the party, which helps explain the popular choice by Barrabás. The preparation mentioned at the end refers to the day before the Sabbath, which shows the urgency of the burial before the sabbatical rest. The notes also note that the Jewish council had no authority to execute capital punishment, so Jesus leads to Pilate.
study.theology: Mark 15 shows the combination of human guilt and divine sovereignty. Jesus is rejected by leaders, crowds and soldiers, but remains silent before accusations and advances to the cross as the true King. The Roman inscription, though intended as an accusation, ends up proclaiming its identity. The cross appears as a place of shame and also of fulfillment of the Scriptures, for Jesus is counted on transgressors. The cry on the cross expresses real abandonment and deep suffering, without ceasing to be prayer. Darkness symbolizes judgment and reveal the sinister character of what occurs. The tear of the veil suggests decisive rupture in the relationship between God and the system of the temple, and the confession of the centurion shows that the death of Jesus produces unexpected recognition of who he is. Careful burial, together with the witness of women, indicates that death does not erase the dignity of Jesus nor closes the hope of the Kingdom.

scholarViews.insight: The expression "King of the Jews" functions as the Gentile equivalent of the title "King of Israel," and Jesus" response to Pilate confirms his royal consciousness, although not as a political threat.
Pilate surrenders Jesus to be crucified to please the crowd, revealing the weakness of authority in the face of popular pressure and the injustice of the process.
The darkness from noon to the ninth hour is presented as a literal and symbolic sign, pointing to judgment and the gravity of what was happening.

questions: What does Jesus' refusal to defend himself teaches about his mission and his trust in God?
In what sense does the cross reveal at the same time human injustice and the fulfillment of God's plan?
How can the example of Joseph of Arimathea and women correct our tendency to retreat when following Jesus costs reputation or safety?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to fidelity amid pressure. Notice where the crowd, leaders, and even soldiers choose convenience instead of the truth, and ask God for the courage not to repeat this pattern. Also imitate Joseph of Arimathea and the women: honor Jesus when this is not popular, take care of what belongs to Christ with reverence, and remain close to him even when the cross seems to be defeat. If you face injustice or silence from God, remember that Jesus also went through it and continued to trust the Father.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not fully resolve the harmonization between the time indicated by Mark and other chronological references of the Gospels. They also do not allow for sure to determine the exact extent of darkness beyond what the text itself states. The theological sense of tearing the veil is interpretive, not directly explained by the chapter.
